title: Vocabulary Lessons
subtitle: Zero to Band 9, the full nextED vocabulary book: 30 Bangla-speaker errors, the 35-word upgrade matrix, 100 verbs and linking words, 15 topic bundles, idioms and register, and the full workbook - every exercise with its answer

chapters.title: The Bangladeshi L1 Interference Fixer
blocks: Most Bangladeshi candidates lose their easiest marks here. The sentences in this chapter are not produced by weak students. They are produced by strong, fluent students whose English is being quietly shaped by Bangla underneath.

Each error below is a faithful translation of a perfectly correct Bangla thought. The Bangla is not the problem. The word-for-word carrying of Bangla structure into English is the problem, and an examiner recognises it instantly.

This is called first-language (L1) interference. It is predictable, it is patterned, and because it is patterned, it is fixable. Work through all thirty errors and note which ones you produce yourself.

Then do the two exercise sets at the end with a pen before checking the key. Each entry gives you five things: the incorrect sentence, the Bangla logic that produces it, the Band 9 correction, the precise grammar or lexical rule, and the examiner’s view of what it costs you.

chapters.title: The 30 core errors (1–10)
blocks: I discussed about the problem with my teacher.
I discussed the problem with my teacher.

Discuss is a transitive verb: it takes a direct object with no preposition after it. The same is true of enter, approach, reach, marry, request, and lack. You discuss a problem, not discuss about a problem. If you want a noun, use have a discussion about.
আমি শিক্ষকের সাথে সমস্যাটি নিয়ে আলোচনা করেছি. The word নিয়ে (niye) carries the sense of “about,” so learners attach about to discuss.

**Examiner view:** This single preposition is one of the most reliable markers of a Bangladeshi script. It falls under both Grammatical Range and Accuracy and Lexical Resource, because it is a collocation error. One instance is a slip; repeated instances signal a fossilised habit and hold you at Band 6.5.
The writer emphasised on the need for reform.
The writer emphasised the need for reform. / The writer placed emphasis on the need for reform.
Emphasise is transitive and takes no preposition. The preposition on belongs only to the noun form: place emphasis on, put stress on. Choose one structure; do not mix them.
লেখক সংস্কারের প্রয়োজনীয়তার উপর জোর দিয়েছেন. জোর দেওয়া (jor deoa, “to give stress”) pairs with উপর (upor, “on”), so on is carried across.

**Examiner view:** This appears constantly in Task 2 essays about what a text or a policy “highlights.” Getting it right shows the examiner you control the verb and noun forms of the same idea, which is exactly the flexibility Band 7 rewards.
We reached to the station just before the train left.
We reached the station just before the train left. / We arrived at the station just in time.
Reach is transitive: reach a place, no preposition. If you prefer arrive, it takes at (a point) or in (a large area): arrive at the station, arrive in Dhaka.
আমরা স্টেশনে পৌঁছেছি. The locative ending ে (-e, “to/at”) on স্টেশন becomes to in English.
**Examiner view:** Reach to is a small error but a frequent one in Speaking Part 2 narratives. Fixing it removes a recurring accuracy penalty from your storytelling.
My cousin is married with a doctor.
My cousin is married to a doctor.
The fixed collocation is married to, never married with. You do something with another person, but you are married to them. Compare engaged to, related to.
আমার চাচাতো ভাইয়ের একজন ডাক্তারের সাথে বিয়ে হয়েছে. সাথে (shathe) means “with,” so with follows married.

**Examiner view:** Relationship vocabulary comes up in Speaking Part 1 (family) constantly. A collocation slip here is minor in isolation but memorable to an examiner listening for natural word partnerships.
My manager is senior than me.
My manager is senior to me. / My manager is more experienced than I am.
A small group of comparative adjectives from Latin take to, not than: senior to, junior to, superior to, inferior to, prior to. Only ordinary comparatives (bigger, faster) take than.
আমার ম্যানেজার আমার থেকে সিনিয়র. থেকে (theke) means both “from” and “than,” so learners use than after senior.

**Examiner view:** Using superior to and prior to correctly is a quiet Band 7.5 signal. It shows awareness of less common lexical items and their collocations, which the band descriptors reward directly.
I prefer reading books than watching television.
I prefer reading books to watching television.

Prefer takes to, not than: prefer A to B. When both options are verbs, keep them in the same form: prefer reading to watching. The alternative structure is would rather read than watch, where than is correct.
আমি টেলিভিশন দেখার থেকে বই পড়া বেশি পছন্দ করি. Again থেকে (theke, “than/from”) pulls in than.

**Examiner view:** Prefer is a very high-frequency Speaking Part 1 verb. The prefer to pattern is one of the most cost-effective fixes in this chapter, because you will use it in almost every interview.
She is very good in mathematics and physics.
She is very good at mathematics and physics.
Skill adjectives take at: good at, skilled at, talented at, poor at. In is used only for a field as a whole in a different structure (a degree in physics).
সে অঙ্ক আর পদার্থবিজ্ঞানে খুব ভালো. The locative ে (-e, “in”) on the subject names becomes in.

**Examiner view:** Describing abilities is unavoidable in Speaking Part 1 (study and work). Good at versus good in is a classic adjective-plus-preposition test, and consistent accuracy here lifts your collocation profile.
My teacher gave me a very useful advice.
My teacher gave me a very useful piece of advice. / My teacher gave me some very useful advice.
Advice is uncountable: no a/an, no plural -s, and a singular verb. To count it, use a partitive: a piece of advice, two pieces of advice.
আমার শিক্ষক আমাকে একটি খুব দরকারি উপদেশ দিয়েছেন. উপদেশ (upodesh, “advice”) is countable in Bangla, so একটি (ekti, “a/one”) is attached.

**Examiner view:** Uncountable-noun control is on the South Asian error checklist for a reason. Writing a advice or advices is an immediate Band 6 word-formation marker; the piece of fix signals you know the rule.
The library provides many informations and equipments.
The library provides a great deal of information and equipment.

Information, equipment, furniture, research, knowledge, accommodation, traffic, and progress are all uncountable in English. They never take -s. Quantify them with a great deal of, a large amount of, or much.
লাইব্রেরি অনেক তথ্য এবং সরঞ্জাম সরবরাহ করে. তথ্য (tottho) and সরঞ্জাম (shoronjam) behave as countable in Bangla, so the English plural -s is added.

**Examiner view:** These eight words appear in almost every academic essay. Pluralising even one of them repeatedly is enough to pull Lexical Resource down to Band 6, because word formation is scored inside that criterion.
I am completely agree with this statement.
I completely agree with this statement. / I am in complete agreement with this statement.
Agree is a full verb, not an adjective. It does not take am/is/are. Either use the verb (I agree) or the noun phrase (I am in agreement). Never am agree.
আমি এই বক্তব্যের সাথে সম্পূর্ণ একমত. একমত (ekmot) is a state of being “in agreement,” which feels like an adjective, so learners add am.

**Examiner view:** Agree-and-disagree essays are the most common Task 2 type. Opening with I am agree in the first sentence signals a Band 5.5 grammar profile before the examiner has read your argument. This is a high-value fix.

chapters.title: The 30 core errors (11–20)
blocks: Everybody in my office are working overtime this week.
Everybody in my office is working overtime this week.

Everybody, everyone, somebody, nobody, each, and neither are grammatically singular and take a singular verb, however many people they describe. The interrupting phrase (in my office) does not change this.
আমার অফিসের সবাই এই সপ্তাহে অতিরিক্ত সময় কাজ করছে. সবাই (shobai, “everybody”) refers to many people, so the verb feels plural.
**Examiner view:** Subject-verb agreement with indefinite pronouns is a frequent Band 6 slip. Because it recurs across a whole script, a single fixed habit here protects marks in every paragraph.
One of my friend is studying in Canada.
One of my friends is studying in Canada.
After one of, the noun must be plural (one of my friends), because you are selecting one from a group. The verb, however, stays singular because the true subject is one: one of my friends is.
আমার এক বন্ধু কানাডায় পড় ছে. এক বন্ধু (ek bondhu, “one friend”) is singular in Bangla, so friend stays singular.
**Examiner view:** This is a two-part trap: plural noun, singular verb. Candidates usually fix one half and miss the other. Getting both right is a clear Band 7 accuracy signal in Speaking Part 1.
Every students must bring their identity card.
Every student must bring their identity card. / All students must bring their identity cards.
Every and each are always followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: every student is. If you want a plural noun, switch the determiner to all: all students are.
প্রত্যেক ছাত্রকে তাদের পরিচয়পত্র আনতে হবে. Bangla nouns are not forced into a plural form, so ছাত্র (chhatro, “student”) is read as flexible.
**Examiner view:** Every plus a plural noun is a basic countability error that caps Grammatical Range and Accuracy quickly. The fix is mechanical once you pair every with singular in your mind.
The number of road accidents are increasing every year.
The number of road accidents is increasing every year.

The subject of this sentence is number (singular), not accidents. The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb. Contrast a number of + plural noun, which means “several” and takes a plural verb: a number of accidents are unreported.
সড় ক দুর্ঘটনার সংখ্যা প্রতি বছর বাড় ছে. The plural idea “accidents” sits right before the verb and pulls it toward plural.
**Examiner view:** This exact phrase, the number of, is a Task 1 workhorse. Getting the agreement right on it is one of the most visible accuracy wins available in a data description.
Despite of the heavy rain, the ceremony continued.
Despite the heavy rain, the ceremony continued. / In spite of the heavy rain, the ceremony continued.
Despite takes no of. In spite of keeps its of. Both are followed by a noun or an -ing form, never a full clause. For a full clause, use although: Although it rained heavily, the ceremony continued.
ভারী বৃষ্টি সত্ত্বেও, অনুষ্ঠান চলতে থাকল. সত্ত্বেও (sotteo) translates as “in spite of,” so learners blend the two and produce despite of.

**Examiner view:** The despite of blend is one of the single most common concession errors in Bangladeshi Task 2 writing. Because concession is a core essay move, this error surfaces often and is worth eliminating completely.
After his studies, he returned back to his hometown.
After his studies, he returned to his hometown.
Return already means “go back,” so returned back is redundant. The same redundancy affects repeat again, revert back, reverse back, and ascend up. Use the single verb.
পড়াশোনা শেষে সে তার নিজ শহরে ফিরে গেছে. ফিরে যাওয়া (phire jaoa) already contains the sense of “returning back,” so back is added on top in English.

**Examiner view:** Redundancy is a Lexical Resource weakness: it shows the meaning of a word has not been fully absorbed. Trimming these doublings makes your writing tighter and more precise, which is exactly the Band 8 quality of “conveying precise meaning.”
Students must learn to cope up with academic pressure.
Students must learn to cope with academic pressure.
The verb is cope with, with no up. The intruding up is a South Asian regional habit. Compare the correct put up with (tolerate), which is a genuinely different phrasal verb.
শিক্ষার্থীদের শিক্ষাগত চাপের সাথে খাপ খাওয়াতে শিখতে হবে. There is no up in the Bangla; the up is added by false analogy with other phrasal verbs like keep up, put up with.

**Examiner view:** Phrasal-verb accuracy is scored under Lexical Resource. Cope up with is instantly recognisable to examiners as a regional error, so removing it sharpens the natural, native quality your Speaking band depends on.
The committee comprises of twelve senior members.
The committee comprises twelve senior members. / The committee is composed of twelve senior members. / The committee consists of twelve senior members.
Comprise is transitive and takes no of. The of belongs to consist of and be composed of. Never mix them into comprises of.
কমিটি বারো জন প্রবীণ সদস্য নিয়ে গঠিত. নিয়ে গঠিত (niye gothito, “formed with/of”) maps to “comprises of.”
**Examiner view:** This is a favourite in Task 1 pie-chart and process descriptions. Choosing consists of or comprises correctly shows control of a less common academic verb, a Band 7 range marker.
I have visited Cox’s Bazar last winter with my family.
I visited Cox’s Bazar last winter with my family.

A finished time expression (last winter, in 2019, two years ago) forces the simple past. The present perfect cannot appear with a stated finished time. Use present perfect only for open or continuing time (I have visited Cox’s Bazar several times).
আমি গত শীতে পরিবারসহ কক্সবাজার গিয়েছি. Conversational Bangla uses one past form for both “I went” and “I have gone,” so the present perfect is over-applied.

**Examiner view:** This tense clash is a content-level error in Speaking Part 2, where you narrate a past experience. Consistent past tense across a two-minute talk is a strong fluency and accuracy signal.
I am living in Dhaka since 2015.
I have been living in Dhaka since 2015. / I have lived in Dhaka since 2015.

A duration that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect or present perfect continuous, not the present continuous. The signal words since and for pull you toward the perfect form.
আমি ২০১৫ সাল থেকে ঢাকায় থাকছি. The Bangla continuous থাকছি (thakchhi) covers ongoing duration, so it maps to the English present continuous.
**Examiner view:** Time-frame control separates Band 6 from Band 7 in Speaking Part 1. The have been + -ing since pattern is a high-frequency structure worth drilling until it is automatic.

chapters.title: The 30 core errors (21–30)
blocks: My friend told to me that the interview went well.
My friend told me that the interview went well. / My friend said to me that the interview went well.
Tell takes a person directly with no to (tell me, tell him). Say needs to before a person (say to me). The two verbs pattern differently: tell someone something versus say something to someone.
আমার বন্ধু আমাকে বলল যে সাক্ষাৎকারটি ভালো হয়েছে. আমাকে বলল (amake bollo, “told me”) includes a “to me” sense that gets spelled out in English.

**Examiner view:** Reported speech runs through Speaking Part 2 narratives. The tell/say split is a precise lexical distinction, and controlling it reads as genuine command of high-frequency reporting verbs.
According to me, the voting age should be lowered.
In my opinion, the voting age should be lowered. / To my mind, the voting age should be lowered.
According to introduces an external source (according to the report, according to experts), not your own view. For your own view, use in my opinion, from my perspective, or I would argue that.
আমার মতে, ভোটের বয়স কমানো উচিত. আমার মতে (amar mote) is a fixed phrase for “in my opinion,” and it maps too literally onto “according to me.”

**Examiner view:** According to me is one of the most frequent opinion-phrase errors in Bangladeshi Task 2 essays and Speaking Part 3. Replacing it with a varied set of opinion markers lifts both Lexical Resource and the academic register examiners expect.
Maximum people in my country depend on agriculture.
Most people in my country depend on agriculture. / The majority of people in my country depend on agriculture.
Maximum is a noun or adjective meaning the highest possible amount (the maximum speed). It does not mean “most.” For the greater part of a group, use most, the majority of, or the bulk of.
আমার দেশের বেশিরভাগ মানুষ কৃষির উপর নির্ভর করে. বেশিরভাগ (beshirbhag, “most”) is mistranslated as “maximum.”
**Examiner view:** Maximum people is a clear word-choice error under Lexical Resource. Swapping it for the majority of or the bulk of also gives you the range of quantifiers that Task 2 rewards.
I have to give an important exam at the end of this month.
I have to sit an important exam at the end of this month. / I have to take an important exam at the end of this month.
In English, a student sits or takes an exam; only the examiner or institution sets or gives one. Give an exam reverses the roles.
এই মাসের শেষে আমাকে একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ পরীক্ষা দিতে হবে. পরীক্ষা দেওয়া (porikkha deoa, “to give an exam”) uses দেওয়া (deoa, “give”), so learners say “give an exam.”
**Examiner view:** Education vocabulary is central to Speaking Part 1. Sit an exam (British usage, favoured in IELTS) is a natural collocation that immediately reads as more native than give an exam.
Try not to do the same mistake in the next test.
Try not to make the same mistake in the next test.

English splits do and make by collocation. You make a mistake, a decision, progress, an effort, an arrangement; you do homework, research, a favour, business, damage. Bangla করা covers all of these, so the split must be learned as fixed pairs.
পরের পরীক্ষায় একই ভুল কোরো না. ভুল করা (bhul kora) uses করা (kora), which covers both “do” and “make,” so do a mistake results.
**Examiner view:** The do/make division is one of the highest-frequency collocation tests in the language. Consistent accuracy is a strong Lexical Resource signal; frequent slips cap you at Band 6.
I have not met my school friends since a long time.
I have not met my school friends for a long time.

Since is followed by a point in time when something began (since 2015, since Monday). For is followed by a length of time (for a long time, for three years). “A long time” is a duration, so it takes for.
আমি অনেকদিন ধরে আমার স্কুলের বন্ধুদের সাথে দেখা করিনি. ধরে (dhore) marks a stretch of time and is loosely read as “since.”

**Examiner view:** The since/for distinction pairs directly with the present perfect from Error 20. Mastering both together removes a cluster of related errors that otherwise recur throughout Speaking Part 1.
Please off the fan and light before you leave the room.
Please turn off the fan and the light before you leave the room.
English uses the phrasal verbs turn on and turn off (or switch on/off) for electrical devices. Off is not a verb, and open/close apply to doors and windows, not to lights and fans.
ঘর ছাড়ার আগে ফ্যান আর লাইট বন্ধ করো. বন্ধ করা (bondho kora, “to close/shut off”) becomes “off,” and খোলা (khola, “to open”) becomes “open,” giving off the fan, open the light.

**Examiner view:** Open the light and off the fan are unmistakable regional calques. They rarely appear in Writing but surface in Speaking Part 1 about home and daily routine, where natural phrasal verbs are exactly what the examiner is listening for.
My all relatives gathered for the wedding celebration.
All my relatives gathered for the wedding celebration.
In English, all comes before the possessive: all my relatives, all his money, all our efforts. The Bangla order “my all” is reversed. The same holds for both my parents, half my salary.
আমার সব আত্মীয় বিয়ের অনুষ্ঠানে জড়ো হয়েছিল. আমার সব (amar shob, literally “my all”) places the possessive before all, and the order carries over.

**Examiner view:** Determiner order is a subtle Grammatical Range and Accuracy point. It is minor in isolation but, when consistent, contributes to the smooth, natural flow that distinguishes higher-band speech and writing.
Myself Rahim, and I am here to talk about my hometown.
My name is Rahim, and I am here to talk about my hometown. / I am Rahim, and I would like to talk about my hometown.
Myself is a reflexive pronoun (I did it myself); it cannot introduce a name. Use My name is or I am followed by the name.
আমি রহিম, আর আমি আমার শহর নিয়ে কথা বলতে এসেছি. The self-introduction habit of announcing oneself becomes the non-standard “Myself Rahim.”

**Examiner view:** In the IELTS Speaking test you are not required to introduce yourself formally, but if you do, Myself Rahim is an instant regional marker. The natural I am Rahim sets a stronger first impression on fluency and lexis.
I passed out from university in 2019 with a degree in economics.
I graduated from university in 2019 with a degree in economics.
In standard English, pass out means to faint or lose consciousness. To complete a degree, use graduate from or complete my studies at. This is a false friend, not a grammar error.
This is an institutional-English habit rather than a direct Bangla translation: “pass out” is widely used across South Asia to mean “graduate.”

**Examiner view:** Passed out from university can genuinely confuse an examiner, because the standard meaning is “fainted.” Since education background is asked in almost every Speaking Part 1, replacing it with graduated from protects clarity and register at the same time.

chapters.title: Practice · Spot and fix the L1 errors
blocks: Attempt both exercises fully with a pen before checking the answer key. Do not read the key first; recognition is not the same as production.

blocks.title: Exercise 1.1 · Spot the L1 Error
blocks.instructions: Each of the following fifteen sentences contains one hidden Bangla-to-English translation error. Underline the error and rewrite the sentence in correct, natural English.

items.prompt: Scientists are still discussing about the real causes of climate change.
items.answer: Scientists are still discussing the real causes of climate change.
items.reason: discuss is transitive and takes its object directly; discuss about doubles a meaning the verb already carries.

items.prompt: This report comprises of five main sections and a short appendix.
items.answer: This report comprises five main sections and a short appendix. (or consists of)
items.reason: comprise takes no of; the of belongs only to consist of and be composed of.

items.prompt: My elder brother is senior than me by four years.
items.answer: My elder brother is senior to me by four years.
items.reason: Latin-origin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, prior) take to, never than.

items.prompt: My sister is married with a civil engineer from Khulna.
items.answer: My sister is married to a civil engineer from Khulna.
items.reason: the fixed collocation is married to; with is used for doing something alongside a person, not for the marriage bond.

items.prompt: I have been staying in this hostel since my first year, and I am living here still now.
items.answer: I have been staying in this hostel since my first year, and I still live here.
items.reason: a situation that began in the past and continues now needs the present perfect, not the present continuous.

items.prompt: The counsellor gave me two very useful advices about choosing a subject.
items.answer: The counsellor gave me two very useful pieces of advice about choosing a subject.
items.reason: advice is uncountable, so it cannot take a plural -s; to count it, use pieces of advice.

items.prompt: Everyone in our study group are preparing hard for the mock test.
items.answer: Everyone in our study group is preparing hard for the mock test.
items.reason: everyone is grammatically singular, however many people it refers to; the phrase in our study group does not change the verb.

items.prompt: Despite of the heavy workload, she submitted every assignment on time.
items.answer: Despite the heavy workload, she submitted every assignment on time.
items.reason: despite takes no of; only in spite of keeps the of.

items.prompt: According to me, public libraries should stay open late into the evening.
items.answer: In my opinion, public libraries should stay open late into the evening.
items.reason: according to introduces an external source, not your own view; use in my opinion for yourself.

items.prompt: The number of private cars on the road are rising sharply each year.
items.answer: The number of private cars on the road is rising sharply each year.
items.reason: the true subject is number (singular); the number of always takes a singular verb.

items.prompt: It is difficult for many workers to cope up with rapid technological change.
items.answer: It is difficult for many workers to cope with rapid technological change.
items.reason: the verb is cope with; the extra up is a regional habit with no basis in the phrase.

items.prompt: Please open the light; the room is too dark to read in.
items.answer: Please turn on the light; the room is too dark to read in.
items.reason: lights and devices are turned on or off; open/close apply to doors and windows.

items.prompt: We reached to the examination hall twenty minutes before it started.
items.answer: We reached the examination hall twenty minutes before it started. (or arrived at)
items.reason: reach is transitive and takes no preposition; arrive takes at or in.

items.prompt: Most students prefer group study than studying alone at home.
items.answer: Most students prefer group study to studying alone at home.
items.reason: prefer pairs with to, not than; keep both options in the same form (study to studying).

items.prompt: After completing his research, he returned back to his home country.
items.answer: After completing his research, he returned to his home country.
items.reason: return already means “go back,” so back is redundant.

blocks.title: Exercise 1.2 · Bangla to Band 9 Translation Challenge
blocks.instructions: Read each Bangla thought and write one natural, error-free IELTS sentence that expresses it. Do not translate word by word; translate the meaning. Each thought hides at least one of the traps from Part A.

items.prompt: বেশিরভাগ মানুষ মনে করে যে প্রযুক্তি আমাদের দৈনন্দিন জীবনকে অনেক সহজ করেছে।
items.answer: Most people believe that technology has made our daily lives much easier.
items.reason: Trap: maximum for most; use the present perfect for a change with present relevance.

items.prompt: যানজট সত্ত্বেও, শহরের বেশিরভাগ মানুষ এখনও ব্যক্তিগত গাড়ি ব্যবহার করতে পছন্দ করে।
items.answer: Despite the traffic congestion, most city dwellers still prefer to use private cars.
items.reason: Trap: despite of; prefer … to.

items.prompt: আমার মতে, সরকারের উচিত শিক্ষা খাতে আরও বেশি বিনিয়োগ করা।
items.answer: In my opinion, the government should invest more heavily in the education sector.
items.reason: Trap: according to me; invest in.

items.prompt: আমি ২০১৮ সাল থেকে এই বিষয়ের উপর গবেষণা করছি।
items.answer: I have been researching this subject since 2018.
items.reason: Trap: present continuous with since; research is transitive, no about.

items.prompt: দূষণ জনস্বাস্থ্যের জন্য একটি মারাত্মক হুমকি সৃষ্টি করছে।
items.answer: Pollution poses a serious threat to public health.
items.reason: Trap: use the precise collocation pose a threat to rather than a vague verb.

items.prompt: তরুণ প্রজন্মের জন্য কর্মসংস্থানের সুযোগ তৈরি করা অত্যন্ত জরুরি।
items.answer: It is essential to create employment opportunities for the younger generation.
items.reason: Trap: formal it is essential to; natural phrase the younger generation.

items.prompt: যদিও অনেক শিক্ষার্থী ইংরেজিতে ভালো, তবুও তারা পরীক্ষায় ভালো ফল করতে পারে না।
items.answer: Although many students are good at English, they fail to perform well in the exam.
items.reason: Trap: good in to good at; although with a full clause.

items.prompt: আমি একদিন আমার নিজের একটি প্রতিষ্ঠান গড়ে তুলতে চাই।
items.answer: I hope to build my own company one day.
items.reason: Trap: natural build/establish a company and hope to, not a word-for-word translation.

items.prompt: দারিদ্র্য দূর করা যেকোনো উন্নয়নশীল দেশের সবচেয়ে বড় চ্যালেঞ্জ।
items.answer: Eradicating poverty is the biggest challenge for any developing nation.
items.reason: Trap: eradicate upgrades remove; a gerund subject.

items.prompt: যদি সরকার আরও কঠোর আইন প্রণয়ন করত, তাহলে অপরাধের হার কমে যেত।
items.answer: If the government enacted stricter laws, the crime rate would decrease.
items.reason: Trap: second conditional (past after if, would in the result); the crime rate, not the rate of crime are.

chapters.title: The Band Upgrade Matrix
blocks: Chapter 1 removed the errors that pull you down. This chapter adds the precision that pushes you up. Every candidate arrives with a small set of overused words that do too much work: big, good, bad, very, problem, thing.

These words are not wrong. They are simply vague, and vagueness is what caps Lexical Resource at Band 6. The examiner is not impressed by a rare word for its own sake; the examiner is impressed by the right word, the one that says exactly what you mean.

For thirty-five of the most overworked words in Bangladeshi English, this chapter gives you a ladder: the Band 5.5 version you probably use now, a Band 7.5 upgrade, and a Band 9.0 precision choice, with clear instructions on where each belongs. Read the whole entry, not just the fancy word at the top, because the usage rule and the Speaking-versus-Writing split are what protect you from the single most common trap at this level: dropping a heavy academic word into the wrong place. A warning before you start.

Do not try to use every Band 9.0 word in every sentence. A script stuffed with plethora, myriad, and paradigm reads as memorised and unnatural, and examiners penalise exactly that. The skill is selection: one precise word where a vague one used to sit.
Range plus accuracy, not range at the cost of it.

chapters.title: The upgrade matrix (1–9: big … beautiful)
blocks: Dhaka is a big city with a big population.

large, major, significant, substantial, considerable. “Dhaka has a substantial population and faces major infrastructure pressure.” Use large for physical size, substantial and considerable for amounts, major and significant for importance.
immense, profound, monumental. Reserve these for genuine scale or impact: immense for sheer size, profound for a deep effect (a profound impact on society), monumental for a huge task or achievement.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, huge and massive sound natural and are fine. In Writing Task 2, avoid big, huge, and massive; use substantial, significant, or considerable.
বড় (boro) covers size, age, and importance in one word, so learners use big for all three. English separates them: large for size, elder or older for age, significant for importance.
Only a small number of people supported the plan.
minor, slight, modest, limited. “A modest proportion of respondents supported the plan.” Use slight for a small degree of change, minor for low importance, modest and limited for small amounts.
negligible, marginal, minimal. Negligible means so small it can be ignored; marginal means barely significant; minimal means the least possible.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, tiny and little are natural. In Writing, prefer slight, minor, or marginal, especially in Task 1 for describing small changes (a marginal increase).
ছোট (chhoto) spans size, age, and low importance. English needs small (size), younger (age), and minor or trivial (importance).
Public transport is good for the environment.

beneficial, positive, effective, favourable. “Public transport has a positive effect on air quality.” Use beneficial for something that helps, effective for something that works, favourable for conditions or outcomes.
advantageous, invaluable, conducive. Invaluable means extremely useful; conducive to means it helps bring something about (conducive to learning).
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, great and really useful are natural. In Writing, beneficial and advantageous carry the academic tone; never write a good thing in Task 2.
ভালো (bhalo) means good, well, kind, and fine all at once, so good gets overused. English splits it: good (quality), well (adverb), kind (a person), fine (acceptable).
Smoking is very bad for your health.
harmful, negative, damaging, poor. “Smoking is extremely harmful to health.” Use harmful and damaging for physical harm, negative for effects and attitudes, poor for low quality (poor performance).
detrimental, adverse, deleterious. Detrimental to and adverse effect on are the strong academic collocations for harm.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, terrible and awful are natural. In Writing, use detrimental or adverse; write a detrimental effect on health, not a bad effect.
খারাপ (kharap) covers bad, evil, spoiled, and poor-quality. English chooses by context: harmful (to health), poor (quality), unpleasant (experience).
Education is very important for a country.
significant, crucial, essential, key. “Education plays a crucial role in national development.” Use essential for something you cannot do without, crucial and key for something decisive.
vital, paramount, pivotal, indispensable. Paramount means most important of all; pivotal means central to how something turns out; indispensable means absolutely necessary.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, really important is fine. In Writing, rotate crucial, vital, and essential so you do not repeat one word across paragraphs.
গুরুত্বপূর্ণ (gurutwopurno) is a single high-frequency word, so learners rarely vary it. English offers a whole scale from significant up to paramount.
Learning a new language is very difficult.

challenging, demanding, tough, complex. “Mastering a new language is a demanding process.” Use challenging for something hard but rewarding, demanding for something that takes effort, complex for something complicated.
arduous, formidable, daunting. Arduous means long and tiring; formidable means seriously difficult to overcome; daunting means intimidating to face.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, hard and tricky are natural. In Writing, challenging and complex are safe and academic; save arduous and daunting for genuine difficulty.
কঠিন (kothin) means hard, tough, and strict together. English separates difficult (a task), hard (informal), and strict (a person or rule).
Air pollution is very dangerous for children.
harmful, hazardous, risky, unsafe. “Air pollution is hazardous to young children.” Use hazardous for materials and conditions, risky for actions, unsafe for environments.
perilous, detrimental, life-threatening. Detrimental to health is the standard essay collocation; perilous and life-threatening are reserved for genuine danger to life.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, really dangerous is fine. In Writing, hazardous and detrimental fit the academic register; do not overuse perilous, which is dramatic.
বিপজ্জনক (bipojjonok) covers dangerous and risky without distinction. English separates dangerous (could cause harm) from risky (involves a chance of loss).
Rich countries should help poor countries.
wealthy, affluent, well-off, high-income. “Affluent nations should support developing ones.” Use affluent for people and societies, high-income for a formal economic label.
prosperous, opulent, well-to-do. Prosperous suggests thriving and successful (a prosperous economy); opulent suggests visible luxury.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, well-off is natural. In Writing, affluent and prosperous are the academic choices; developed nations is often more precise than rich countries.
ধনী (dhoni) means wealthy, while সমৃদ্ধ (somriddho) means prosperous or abundant. Choosing prosperous over rich signals you can match the exact shade of meaning.
attractive, stunning, scenic, charming. “Bangladesh has many scenic landscapes.” Use scenic for natural views, charming for towns and villages, stunning for something visually striking.
picturesque, breathtaking, idyllic. Picturesque means as pretty as a picture; breathtaking means astonishingly beautiful; idyllic means peaceful and perfect.
**Speaking vs Writing:** These are mostly Speaking words, useful in Part 2 when describing a place. In Writing they appear rarely, mainly in tourism topics.
সুন্দর (shundor) is used for scenery, people, objects, and experiences alike. English chooses a different word for each: scenic (views), attractive (appearance), elegant (design).

chapters.title: The upgrade matrix (10–18: happy … cause (verb))
blocks: I felt very happy when I passed the exam.
pleased, glad, content, satisfied. “I was extremely pleased to pass the exam.” Use content and satisfied for lasting states, pleased and glad for reactions.
delighted, elated, gratified, overjoyed. Delighted is strong pleasure; elated and overjoyed are intense, short-lived joy; gratified is quiet satisfaction at a deserved result.
**Speaking vs Writing:** These are chiefly Speaking words, essential for Part 2 narratives about feelings. In Writing they appear in wellbeing and quality-of-life topics.
খুশি (khushi) is momentary gladness, while সুখী (shukhi) is deep, lasting happiness. English mirrors this with pleased (momentary) versus content (lasting).
History is a very interesting subject.
engaging, appealing, fascinating, absorbing. “History is a fascinating field of study.” Use engaging for something that holds attention, appealing for something attractive to many.
captivating, compelling, riveting, intriguing. Compelling means so interesting it convinces you; riveting means you cannot look away; intriguing means interesting because mysterious.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, fascinating works everywhere. In Writing, compelling is especially useful (a compelling argument, compelling evidence).
মজার (mojar) means fun or amusing, while আকর্ষণীয় (akorshoniyo) means attractive or interesting. Learners often use interesting for both; English separates fun from fascinating.
The price of food increased a lot last year.
rise, grow, climb, expand. “Food prices rose sharply last year.” Use grow for gradual expansion, climb for steady upward movement.
surge, soar, escalate, rocket. Surge and soar mean a sudden, large rise; escalate means to intensify, often something negative (escalating tensions).
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing Task 1 these are essential and must be varied. In Speaking, go up is natural and acceptable. Match strength to the data: use surge only for a dramatic rise.
বাড়া (bara, intransitive) and বাড়ানো (barano, transitive) both translate as “increase,” so learners miss the English split between rise (no object) and raise (needs an object).
The number of readers decreased over time.
decline, fall, drop, reduce. “Readership declined steadily over the decade.” Remember: decline, fall, and drop take no object; reduce and lower need one.
plummet, plunge, dwindle, diminish. Plummet and plunge mean a sudden steep fall; dwindle means shrink gradually to almost nothing; diminish means to become less over time.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Task 1, vary fall, decline, and drop across the description. In Speaking, go down is natural.
কমা (koma) and কমানো (komano) again blur the intransitive and transitive forms, producing errors like the price reduced instead of the price fell.
The government must solve the traffic problem.
tackle, address, deal with, resolve. “The government must address the traffic problem.” Use tackle and address for approaching a problem, resolve for settling it fully.
remedy, eradicate, alleviate, mitigate. These carry precise shades: remedy corrects a fault, eradicate removes completely, alleviate eases suffering, mitigate reduces severity.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing Task 2 solution paragraphs, tackle and address are the workhorses. Reserve eradicate for problems that can genuinely be wiped out, such as a disease.
সমাধান করা (shomadhan kora) covers solve and resolve equally, so learners default to solve. English prefers tackle or address when the problem is ongoing and not yet fully solved.
Technology has changed our daily life.
alter, transform, modify, shift. “Technology has transformed daily life.” Use modify for small adjustments, transform for a complete change, shift for a change of direction.
revolutionise, reshape, overhaul, reconfigure. Revolutionise means change radically and for good; overhaul means a thorough restructuring of a system.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, change is fine. In Writing, transform and reshape add force; revolutionise suits genuinely dramatic change, such as the internet.
পরিবর্তন (poriborton) means change in general, while বদলানো (bodlano) can mean exchange or swap. English distinguishes change (become different) from exchange (swap one for another).
The internet helps students to learn faster.
assist, support, aid, enable. “The internet enables students to learn more efficiently.” Use enable when the help makes something possible, support for ongoing help.
facilitate, foster, bolster. Facilitate means make a process easier; foster means encourage growth or development; bolster means strengthen.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, help is natural and correct. In Writing, facilitate and foster carry the academic tone (foster creativity, facilitate communication).
সাহায্য করা (shahajjo kora) covers help, assist, and aid without distinction. English chooses facilitate for processes and foster for growth, which are not interchangeable.
The graph shows that sales increased in 2020.
demonstrate, reveal, indicate, display. “The graph indicates a rise in sales in 2020.” Use indicate for data pointing to a conclusion, reveal for uncovering something not obvious.
illustrate, highlight, underscore, depict. Illustrate is ideal for Task 1 (the chart illustrates); highlight and underscore mean to draw attention to something important.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing Task 1, rotate illustrate, show, indicate, and depict to avoid repetition in the opening line. In Speaking, show is fine.
দেখানো (dekhano) means show or display, so learners default to show. English separates demonstrate (prove through evidence) from display (put on view).
lead to, result in, bring about, contribute to. “Deforestation leads to serious environmental problems.” Use contribute to when it is one cause among several.
trigger, generate, give rise to, precipitate. Trigger means set off suddenly; give rise to is a formal essay phrase; precipitate means bring on abruptly.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing, lead to, result in, and give rise to are core cause-and-effect phrases. In Speaking, cause and lead to are natural.
ঘটানো (ghotano) and সৃষ্টি করা (srishti kora) mean cause or create. English prefers lead to and result in for consequences, keeping create for making something new.

chapters.title: The upgrade matrix (19–27: improve … thing)
blocks: enhance, boost, develop, strengthen. “Regular exercise enhances overall health.” Use enhance to raise quality, boost to raise level or amount, strengthen to make more robust.
refine, optimise, bolster, augment. Refine means improve through small precise changes; optimise means make as effective as possible; augment means add to.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing, enhance and boost are the reliable upgrades. In Speaking, get better and improve are natural.
উন্নতি করা (unnoti kora) covers improve, develop, and progress together, so learners repeat improve. English separates enhance (quality) from develop (grow over time).
Social media affects young people a lot.
influence, impact, shape, have an effect on. “Social media strongly influences young people.” Remember the spelling split: affect is the verb, effect the noun.
undermine, transform, condition. For negative effects, undermine (weaken gradually) is precise; condition means shape behaviour over time.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing, influence and have a significant impact on are safe and formal. Avoid the common Task 2 error impact on used as a verb; write have an impact on.
প্রভাবিত করা (probhabito kora) means affect or influence. Because the noun প্রভাব (probhab) is so close, learners confuse affect and effect; hold the rule: affect acts, effect is the result.
Farmers use modern machines to grow more crops.
utilise, employ, apply, make use of. “Farmers employ modern machinery to raise yields.” Use employ and apply for methods and techniques.
harness, exploit, leverage. Harness means put a natural force to use (harness solar energy); exploit means make full use of a resource; leverage means use something for maximum advantage.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, use is natural; utilise can sound stiff. In Writing, employ and harness fit the academic register.
ব্যবহার করা (byabohar kora) means use in every sense. English adds nuance: harness (a force), exploit (a resource, sometimes negatively).
Students can get good jobs after graduation.
obtain, receive, gain, achieve. “Graduates can obtain well-paid jobs.” Get is too informal and vague for writing; choose the verb that matches the object.
acquire, attain, secure, earn. Acquire suits skills and knowledge; attain suits goals and standards; secure suits something hard to get (secure a scholarship).
**Speaking vs Writing:** Get is fine and natural throughout Speaking. In Writing Task 2, replace every get with a precise verb; get is one of the clearest Band 6 markers in an essay.
পাওয়া (paoa) covers get, obtain, receive, and find. English forces a choice: you acquire a skill, receive a gift, obtain permission, achieve a goal.
Many young people want to work abroad.
wish to, hope to, intend to, would like to. “Many young people hope to work abroad.” Use intend to for a firm plan, wish to for a formal desire.
aspire to, seek to, desire, long to. Aspire to suits ambitions (aspire to leadership); seek to is a formal way to state a purpose.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, want to is natural. In Writing, aspire to and seek to raise the register (students who aspire to higher education).
চাওয়া (chaoa) means want, wish, and ask for. English separates want (desire) from ask for (request), and adds aspire for ambition.
I think that mobile phones are useful.
believe, consider, feel, hold the view that. “I believe that mobile phones are indispensable.” Use consider for a reasoned judgement, feel for a softer opinion.
contend, maintain, be convinced that, argue. Contend and maintain mean assert firmly in an argument, ideal for a Task 2 thesis statement.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, I think and I reckon are natural. In Writing, vary I believe, I would argue, and in my view so you do not open every paragraph with I think.
মনে করা (mone kora) and ভাবা (bhaba) both mean think or believe. English distinguishes think (general) from believe (conviction) and consider (weigh up).
Unemployment is a big problem in many countries.

issue, difficulty, concern, challenge. “Unemployment is a pressing issue in many countries.” Use issue for a matter under debate, concern for something worrying, challenge for a problem worth overcoming.
obstacle, dilemma, predicament, crisis. Obstacle blocks progress; dilemma is a hard choice between options; crisis is a severe, urgent problem.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing, rotate issue, challenge, and concern; do not repeat problem. In Speaking, problem is acceptable but issue sounds more mature.
সমস্যা (shomossha) is the single word for every kind of problem, so learners never vary it. English scales from issue (mild) to crisis (severe).
Pollution has a bad effect on health.
impact, influence, outcome, result. “Pollution has a serious impact on health.” Use impact for a strong effect, outcome and result for what follows from a cause.
consequence, repercussion, ramification, implication. Consequence is a direct result; repercussion is an indirect after-effect; ramification is a complex knock-on effect.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing, impact and consequence are core. Watch the spelling: the noun is effect (a positive effect), not affect.
প্রভাব (probhab) means effect, influence, and impact together. English separates effect (result) from influence (ongoing power to shape).
The most important thing is a good education.
factor, aspect, element, feature. “The most important factor is a sound education.” Thing has no place in academic writing; name what you mean.
phenomenon, component, dimension, consideration. Phenomenon names an observed trend; dimension names one side of a complex issue.
**Speaking vs Writing:** Thing is acceptable in Speaking but weak; in Writing it is a clear Band 6 marker. Replace every thing with factor, aspect, or element.
জিনিস (jinish) means object and ব্যাপার (byapar) means matter or affair. Both collapse into thing in learner English. Choose the specific noun instead.

chapters.title: The upgrade matrix (28–35: way … common)
blocks: There are many ways to reduce pollution.
method, approach, means, strategy. “There are several effective methods of reducing pollution.” Use approach for an overall attitude, strategy for a planned course of action.
mechanism, avenue, measure, initiative. Measure is ideal in solution paragraphs (stringent measures); avenue means a possible route to a goal.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Writing, method, approach, and measure replace way. In Speaking, way is natural (a good way to relax).
উপায় (upay, “means”) and পথ (poth, “road/path”) both surface as way. English separates the literal road from the figurative method or approach.
The government spends a lot of money on defence.
funds, finances, spending, budget. “The government allocates substantial funds to defence.” Use funds for money set aside for a purpose, expenditure for money spent.
capital, resources, revenue, expenditure. Capital is money for investment; revenue is income; expenditure is formal for spending.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, money is fine. In Writing, prefer funds, expenditure, and resources, especially in economy and government-spending essays.
টাকা (taka) is money as cash, while অর্থ (ortho) means wealth or finance. English distinguishes money (general) from capital, funds, and revenue by economic role.
This issue is very important and very serious.

highly, extremely, particularly, considerably. “This issue is highly significant and extremely serious.” Very plus a weak adjective is a Band 6 pattern; upgrade the adjective instead (very important becomes crucial).
profoundly, exceptionally, remarkably, acutely. Acutely aware, profoundly influenced, exceptionally rare: match the adverb to its natural partner.

**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, really and so are natural. In Writing, replace very with a stronger adjective, not just a stronger adverb: very big to substantial, not very big to extremely big.
খুব (khub) and অনেক (onek) attach to almost anything, so very is over-attached in English. The higher-band move is to choose a single strong word rather than intensify a weak one.
A lot of people use public transport every day.

numerous, a large number of, a great deal of, a significant proportion of. “A significant proportion of the population relies on public transport.” Match the quantifier to the noun: a great deal of with uncountables, numerous with countables.
a multitude of, a wealth of, countless, an abundance of. Use these sparingly; one well-placed a wealth of experience is stronger than a lot of repeated.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, a lot of and loads of are natural. In Writing, numerous and a significant proportion of raise precision, especially in Task 1 data description.
অনেক (onek) and বহু (bohu) cover both “many” (countable) and “much” (uncountable). English forces the split: many books, much information.
traditional, long-established, former, aged. “Many long-established traditions are fading.” Use traditional for customs, former for a previous state, elderly for people.
antiquated, outdated, time-honoured, obsolete. Antiquated and obsolete mean out of date; time-honoured means respected because it is old.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, old is fine, but use elderly for people out of politeness. In Writing, traditional, outdated, and long-established carry precise meaning.
পুরনো (purono, “old things”) and বৃদ্ধ (briddho, “old people”) are separate words in Bangla, yet learners use old for both. English politely prefers elderly for people.
New technology has made life easier.
modern, recent, contemporary, emerging. “Emerging technologies have simplified daily life.” Use emerging for something newly appearing, contemporary for present- day.
innovative, cutting-edge, novel, state-of-the-art. Innovative means new and creative; cutting-edge and state-of-the-art mean the most advanced available; novel means new in kind.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, new and the latest are natural. In Writing, innovative and emerging add force, especially in technology essays.
নতুন (notun) means new, fresh, recent, and modern together. English separates recent (in time) from innovative (in originality).
He is a very famous scientist in our country.
well-known, prominent, popular, leading. “He is a prominent scientist in our country.” Use prominent and leading for respected importance, popular for wide liking.
renowned, eminent, distinguished, celebrated. Renowned and eminent mean widely respected for achievement; celebrated means publicly praised.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, famous is natural. In Writing, prominent, renowned, and eminent are the academic choices; famous can sound casual in an essay.
বিখ্যাত (bikkhato, “famous for achievement”) and জনপ্রিয় (jonopriyo, “popular/liked”) are distinct in Bangla. English matches them with renowned versus popular, which are not the same.
It is common to see people using smartphones everywhere.
widespread, frequent, usual, typical. “Smartphone use has become widespread.” Use widespread for something found over a large area, typical for something representative.
prevalent, ubiquitous, pervasive, commonplace. Prevalent means common in a place or time; ubiquitous means found everywhere; pervasive means spreading through every part.
**Speaking vs Writing:** In Speaking, common is fine. In Writing, prevalent and widespread are precise (obesity is prevalent among children).
সাধারণ (shadharon, “ordinary/usual”) and প্রচলিত (procholito, “in current use/widespread”) differ in Bangla. English separates common (ordinary) from prevalent (widely occurring).

chapters.title: Practice · Upgrade and match
blocks: Attempt both exercises with a pen before checking the key.

blocks.title: Exercise 2.1 · Lexical Upgrade Drill
blocks.instructions: Rewrite each Band 5.5 sentence as one natural Band 8.5 to 9.0 sentence, replacing the overused words with precise upgrades from the matrix. Keep the meaning; do not force in more than one or two advanced words per sentence.

items.prompt: Pollution is a very big problem, and the government must solve it fast.
items.answer: Pollution is a pressing issue that the government must tackle urgently.
items.reason: Upgrade: big problem to pressing issue; solve fast to tackle urgently.

items.prompt: The internet is a good thing because it helps students a lot.
items.answer: The internet is highly beneficial because it enables students to learn far more efficiently.
items.reason: Upgrade: good thing to highly beneficial.

items.prompt: Many people think that money is very important for a happy life.
items.answer: Many people believe that financial security is essential to a contented life.
items.reason: Upgrade: money/important/happy all upgraded.

items.prompt: Climate change is a very dangerous thing, and it affects many countries.
items.answer: Climate change is a grave threat that affects numerous countries.
items.reason: Upgrade: very dangerous thing to grave threat.

items.prompt: New technology has changed our life and made many things easy.
items.answer: Emerging technologies have transformed our lives and simplified countless tasks.
items.reason: Upgrade: new technology/changed upgraded.

items.prompt: Rich countries should help poor countries to reduce poverty.
items.answer: Affluent nations should support developing countries in reducing poverty.
items.reason: Upgrade: rich/poor countries/help upgraded.

items.prompt: Tourism is good for the economy, but it can also be bad for the environment.
items.answer: Tourism is beneficial to the economy, yet it can also be detrimental to the environment.
items.reason: Upgrade: good for/bad for upgraded.

items.prompt: Education is a very important way to solve the problem of unemployment.
items.answer: Education is a crucial means of addressing unemployment.
items.reason: Upgrade: very important way/solve the problem of upgraded.

items.prompt: Big cities have a lot of traffic, and this causes many problems.

chapters.title: The 100 high-impact verbs (1–50)
blocks: Read the columns as a word family. The real power of this table is not memorising past tenses; it is being able to move across a row. If increase (verb) is overused, slide to an increase (noun) or increasing (adjective) and rebuild the sentence. That flexibility is exactly what Lexical Resource rewards.
**preposition**: preposition that most commonly follows the verb or its noun
**-**: there is no common single-word form in that class, or no fixed preposition
Spelling follows British conventions (analyse, emphasise, utilise), which IELTS accepts and expects.

chapters.title: The 100 high-impact verbs (51–100)
blocks: The verb affect has the noun effect, not affect. This is the most examined spelling trap in the language, so read row 5 twice: you affect something (verb), and the effect is the result (noun).

Most rows let you paraphrase by shifting class. “The policy improved education” can become “the policy led to an improvement in education” or “the policy had a beneficial effect on education.” Practise sliding along a row until it is automatic; it is the engine of paraphrase in Chapter 5.

chapters.title: The linking word upgrade guide
blocks: Cohesion is scored directly, in the Coherence and Cohesion criterion in Writing and inside Fluency and Coherence in Speaking. Most candidates connect ideas with and, but, so, because, and also. These are not wrong, but a whole script built on them signals Band 6. The fix is a controlled set of higher-level devices, used accurately and not stacked one on top of another.
furthermore, moreover, in addition, additionally, what is more
Renewable energy is clean. Furthermore, it is becoming cheaper each year.
however, nevertheless, in contrast, conversely, on the contrary
The scheme was expensive. Nevertheless, it delivered clear benefits.
notwithstanding, despite this, even so, admittedly, granted that
Notwithstanding the cost, the investment proved worthwhile.
owing to, due to, on account of, as a result of, given that, since
Owing to a shortage of teachers, class sizes have grown.
consequently, therefore, thus, hence, as a result, accordingly
Demand fell sharply; consequently, prices dropped.
Some favour strict rules; conversely, others prefer flexibility.
for instance, to illustrate, namely, such as
Several cities, such as Dhaka and Chittagong, are expanding rapidly.
in conclusion, to sum up, overall, on balance, ultimately
On balance, the advantages outweigh the drawbacks.
“due to” and “owing to” take a noun, not a clause.
Due to the government invested more, education improved.
Owing to greater investment, education improved. / Education improved because the government invested more.
These devices are followed by a noun or noun phrase. If you want a full clause with a subject and verb, use because.
The plan was costly, however, it worked.
The plan was costly. However, it worked. / The plan was costly; however, it worked.
When however joins two complete sentences, it takes a full stop or semicolon before it and a comma after it. A comma alone on both sides creates a comma splice, which is penalised.

One cohesive device per idea is enough. Beginning three sentences in a row with Moreover, Furthermore, In addition is a mechanical overuse that examiners explicitly penalise. Vary the devices, and let some sentences connect through meaning alone. Range means variety, not density.

blocks.title: Exercise 3.2 · Cohesive Device Transformation
blocks.instructions: The paragraph below is written at roughly Band 6.0. Its ideas are sound, but the sentences are short and joined only by basic connectors. Rewrite it as one connected Band 8.0 to 9.0 paragraph, using higher-level cohesive devices accurately and varying them. Do not add new ideas; improve only the linking and flow.

items.prompt: Online education has become very popular. It is cheaper than traditional classes. Students can also study from home. But it has some problems. There is less interaction with teachers. Also, many students lack self-discipline. So, a lot of them do not finish their courses. Online education is useful. But it cannot fully replace the classroom.
items.answer: Online education has grown enormously in popularity, largely because it is cheaper than traditional classes and allows students to study from home. Notwithstanding these advantages, it carries certain drawbacks. To begin with, there is far less interaction with teachers. Moreover, many learners lack the self-discipline that independent study demands; consequently, a significant proportion fail to complete their courses. Online education is therefore undeniably useful, yet it cannot fully replace the classroom.
items.reason: because correctly introduces a full clause, while Notwithstanding is correctly followed by a noun phrase (these advantages), not a clause; the semicolon before consequently joins two related clauses; no device is repeated, so the cohesion is varied rather than mechanical.

chapters.title: Topic-based lexical mastery: how to use the 15 topics
blocks: The fifteen domains in this chapter are the topics IELTS returns to again and again. Whatever the exact question, your Task 2 essay and your Speaking answers will draw on this vocabulary. Each topic gives you a complete bundle: ten academic nouns, ten precise verbs, ten collocations and adjectives, five formal collocations built for Writing Task 2, and five natural idioms built for Speaking.

The line between the last two matters enormously, and Chapter 5 is devoted to it; here, simply notice that the formal set is labelled for Writing and the idiom set for Speaking, and keep them apart. Work each topic, then do its three exercises before checking the answers. A note on the Bangla glosses: they give the everyday meaning of each academic noun so the term is anchored to something you already know.
Do not translate word for word into your essays; use the English term in its natural collocation.

chapters.title: The strict separation rule
blocks: This chapter rests on one rule that decides more Lexical Resource marks than any other single habit: informal idioms belong in Speaking, not in Writing Task 2. The same expression that earns you a point in the interview can cost you one in the essay. This is not a small stylistic preference; it is a register rule, and register is exactly what the higher bands test.

Here is why the split is so sharp. IELTS Speaking rewards natural, spontaneous language, so a well-placed idiom (it was a blessing in disguise, I was over the moon) signals that you can use English the way a fluent speaker actually does. Writing Task 2, by contrast, is a formal academic essay.

In that context an idiom reads as casual, unserious, and out of place, and it pulls your tone down toward Band 6 no matter how impressive the idiom is. The examiner is not asking “does this candidate know idioms.” The examiner is asking “does this candidate know where each kind of language belongs.”
**Safe for Task 2:** Would this sound natural in a newspaper editorial or an academic article? If yes, use it in your essay.
**Keep for Speaking:** Would this sound at home in a friendly chat? If yes, keep it out of Writing Task 2.

**Phrasal verbs:** Many are neutral and perfectly fine in writing (carry out, bring about, result in). The informal, idiomatic ones to keep out of Task 2 are get its act together, cough up, and pull your socks up. When in doubt, choose the single formal verb (organise, pay, improve).

blocks: **tackle the root cause**: to deal with the underlying reason. Example: Lasting change means tackling the root cause.
**implement effective measures**: to put good policies in place. Example: Cities should implement effective measures against pollution.
**a viable solution**: a workable answer. Example: Public transport is a viable solution to congestion.
**weigh the pros and cons**: to consider both sides. Example: Policymakers must weigh the pros and cons.
**strike a balance between**: to find a fair middle. Example: We must strike a balance between growth and conservation.
**take into account**: to consider. Example: Any policy must take into account rural needs.
**a significant proportion of**: a notable share. Example: A significant proportion of graduates work abroad.
**the vast majority of**: almost all. Example: The vast majority of commuters use trains.
**in the long run**: over time. Example: In the long run, prevention is cheaper.
**in the short term**: soon, briefly. Example: In the short term, costs may rise.
**an integral part of**: an essential component. Example: Art is an integral part of education.
**gain momentum**: to grow in strength. Example: The movement has gained momentum.
**pose a serious threat to**: to endanger. Example: Rising seas pose a serious threat to coasts.
**have a detrimental effect on**: to harm. Example: Stress has a detrimental effect on health.
**reap the benefits of**: to enjoy the rewards. Example: Future generations will reap the benefits of this investment.
**at the expense of**: sacrificing something else. Example: Growth should not come at the expense of the environment.
**a case in point**: a fitting example. Example: Singapore is a case in point.
**to illustrate this**: to give an example. Example: To illustrate this, consider public transport in Tokyo.
**bear in mind that**: to remember. Example: We must bear in mind that resources are finite.
**shed light on**: to clarify. Example: The study sheds light on the causes.
**in light of**: considering. Example: In light of these findings, reform is needed.
**from my perspective**: in my opinion. Example: From my perspective, the benefits outweigh the risks.
**more often than not**: usually. Example: More often than not, early action is cheaper.
**by and large**: generally. Example: By and large, the policy has succeeded.
**draw a firm conclusion**: to reach a clear judgement. Example: It is difficult to draw a firm conclusion from limited data.
